title: Who would police the conversion practices ban?
label: · Draft Bill: healthcare and regulation
summary: The committee asked three healthcare regulators how the draft Bill might affect professional standards and investigations. They said they receive very few complaints about conversion practices and already consider such practices incompatible with their professional standards. They broadly favoured limiting the Bill’s healthcare protection to properly regulated professionals and services, but warned that clinical guidance remains contested, online providers may escape oversight, and it is hard to predict how criminal and regulatory processes would interact.

glossary.definition: The body that inspects and regulates many health and care services in England.
The regulator for a range of health and care professions, which sets standards for people on its register.
The UK body that registers doctors and sets standards for their professional conduct.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which publishes guidance on health and care.

chapters.title: What regulators already do
chapters.takeaway: The regulators said complaints in this area are rare, but they already have powers and standards relevant to harmful practice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How well do current rules protect people receiving care related to gender or sexual orientation?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We receive relatively few complaints about doctors in this area. We set professional standards, including clear expectations that doctors explain the risks and benefits of medical treatment and obtain consent.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: The Care Quality Commission regulates services against basic requirements such as safe, respectful care, consent and protecting people from abuse. We’ve taken action where gender services failed those standards, including rating one provider inadequate.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We set standards for the conduct, skills and results expected of the professionals on our register. We receive very few concerns about this subject, and none that I know of about our members engaging in conversion practices.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: These services are contested. Where would you find a common standard for judging what’s reasonable?

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: There are national requirements for children’s and adult services, professional standards, and guidance from colleges and other organisations. Those requirements need updating, but they give us a basis for judging services.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: When we inspect adult gender services, we use those sources to assess whether care is safe and whether abusive practices are taking place.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We’d also look to current clinical guidance. There’s work under way to produce guidance across different professions, but clinical opinion is still divided.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: You’ve had few complaints. Can you actually identify them in your records, or did you have to search manually?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We receive more than 10,000 concerns about doctors each year. Our records don’t have a specific category for this issue, so we manually reviewed cases. I’m fairly confident the number is small.

chapters.title: Who should get the healthcare protection?
chapters.takeaway: All three regulators supported narrowing the draft protection so it covers legitimate, properly regulated healthcare rather than anyone claiming to provide similar care.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Because the Bill allows private prosecutions, do your professional rules need to meet the same test as criminal negligence to protect practitioners?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Our standards describe good professional practice; they aren’t the same as the test for criminal or civil negligence. We rely on clinical guidance from professional bodies and other experts rather than setting that guidance ourselves.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Should the Bill’s healthcare protection be limited to professionals whose work is regulated?

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: Yes. The protection should cover legitimate healthcare. That could mean services we regulate, as well as professionals on approved registers who work to recognised standards.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I agree that the Bill needs a clearer boundary. A broad exemption could be used by people who aren’t providing legitimate healthcare, while regulated professionals need room for difficult, evidence-based conversations.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Regulation gives the public some assurance that a practitioner has training, follows professional standards and can be investigated if concerns arise. The GMC agrees that the protection should be better defined.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: One qualification: our reading is that doctors may not need to rely on this exemption, because the Bill’s other tests may already set a high bar. But I understand why the concerns about the wording matter.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: The Bill also covers procedures similar to medical or surgical care, even when they aren’t treatment for a medical condition. Is it clear who that captures?

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: There are standards for referrals from psychological care to medical treatment and surgery. But I’m not sure exactly which providers that wider wording would include.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I’m not clear what that part is intended to catch or exclude. I’m not a lawyer, and the Bill doesn’t make it obvious.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: Could that wider category include people or services that no regulator oversees?

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: It might. I’d need to check which activities are covered by our rules and write back to the Committee.

chapters.title: Complaints, guidance and gaps in oversight
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses couldn’t predict the effect of the Bill, and warned that some online providers fall outside the regulators’ reach.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Do you know how many therapists in this area aren’t regulated?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: No. We wouldn’t hold that information, particularly about practitioners whose clients wouldn’t come to the General Medical Council.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: The Health and Care Professions Council has guidance referring to the shared agreement against conversion practices. Has that guidance led to more complaints?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We’ve referred to the agreement in our guidance since 2022 and haven’t seen an increase in complaints on this subject. We consider conversion practices incompatible with our standards.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We haven’t seen an increase either. We have a process for dealing with complaints that appear to be vexatious, though deciding that depends on the circumstances.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: We haven’t seen an increase. The Commission isn’t currently a signatory to the shared agreement, but could consider it when it’s reviewed.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: If the Bill passes, do you expect to receive more complaints?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: It’s hard to predict. The Bill may raise awareness, and there are very few complaints now, but we can’t say how the numbers would change.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: Some clinicians have told me they’re worried complaints will rise, but I can’t estimate how likely that is.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: I have the same uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Have you spoken with regulators in countries that already have similar laws?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We reviewed about 27 laws from other countries, with different protections and exceptions, but we haven’t spoken directly to their regulators.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: Some online providers are based overseas and don’t need to register with us. We know of a couple of high-profile examples, but we can’t tell how widespread they are.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: That means there may be people receiving care from providers outside the oversight that applies to services in England.

chapters.title: How criminal cases and regulation might interact
chapters.takeaway: The regulators said a court might consider several sources when deciding whether conduct fell far below expected standards, while their own investigations could reach different outcomes from a criminal trial.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If someone reports abuse and serious harm to the police, how would the healthcare exemption work in court?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: If a doctor on our register is charged, we expect them to tell us. We’d usually let the criminal case run its course rather than start a separate investigation at the same time.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: The Bill makes the healthcare protection depend on whether conduct fell far below expected standards. Is that something regulators already assess for criminal cases?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We have clear professional standards, but they describe good practice. A departure doesn’t automatically mean someone fails our own test. The missing piece is agreement on the clinical guidance that should apply here.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I read the Bill’s wording as drawing on the criminal law. A court might consider a regulator’s standards, but could also look at other evidence. I don’t think the Bill ties the decision to one professional document.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Would a regulator have to give evidence about whether someone’s conduct fell far below the required standard?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We could explain our standards and where professionals can find clinical guidance. Our standards don’t cover every specific situation, so we wouldn’t be making the clinical judgment for the court.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Would you be taking sides in court?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: No. We’d explain our standards as clearly as possible, but an independent expert would more typically give an opinion on the particular conduct.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If someone is acquitted, does that end the matter for the regulators?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Not necessarily. Our question is whether the professional is safe to practise in future, which is different from the criminal test. If someone has understood what went wrong and changed their practice, that may affect our decision.

turns.speaker: Dr Arun Chopra
turns.text: We regulate services rather than individual practitioners. We’d share concerns with the relevant professional regulator and decide whether the service needed inspection or other action.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We could consider regulatory action even after someone wasn’t convicted. We look more broadly at a professional’s conduct than the specific criminal offence.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: A professional body withdrew from the shared agreement over how it applied to children. Do you still rely on that agreement?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I don’t know the details of that decision, so I can’t answer today. I’m happy to look into it and write to the Committee.
